title: AI-powered single-cell imaging and morphology-guided label-free enrichment reveal tumor heterogeneity, genomic relatedness, and divergence in malignant effusions
authors: Magbanua, M. J. M.; Huppert, L. A.; Cruz, J.; Goudreau, J.; Zhou, S.; Yin, K.; Stejskal, P.; Gill, t.; Carelli, R.; Kim, J.; Hsie, L.; Wang, M.; Lian, Z.; Manepalli, S.; Phelan, M.; Ray, M.; Johnson, C.; Nieto, J.; Schneider, E. C.; Mavropoulos, A.; Delson, A. L.; Simmons, C.; Parizadeh, A.; Crawford, J.; Bruck, M.; Her, L.; Barnett, V.; Cabrera, A. M.; Melisko, M.; Balassanian, R.; Rugo, H. S.; van 't Veer, L.; Jovic, A.; Devine, W. P.; Sayaman, R. W.; Salek, M.; Masaeli, M.; Rosenbluth, J.; Goodarzi, H.
abstract: BackgroundMalignant effusions are clinically accessible yet underutilized sources of metastatic tumor cells. However, abundant background immune cells complicate tumor cell isolation and molecular characterization. We integrate AI-powered single-cell imaging and morphology-guided label-free tumor cell enrichment with genomic profiling to characterize phenotypic and genomic heterogeneity in malignant effusions. MethodsWe applied a pre-trained deep learning model to brightfield images of single cells from malignant effusions of 10 patients with metastatic breast cancer to extract morphological features, quantify tumor cell fraction (TCF), and guide label-free microfluidic enrichment. We profiled copy-number alterations and somatic mutations in enriched tumor cell fractions and compared them with available matched effusion cell-free DNA and solid tumors. ResultsAI-powered single-cell morphological analysis identified putative tumor cells in all 10 patients (median TCF, 5.4%; range, 0.51-15.8%; n = 25 samples). AI estimates of major immune-cell populations varied across patients and samples and correlated with flow cytometry measurements (n = 21 paired samples, Pearson r = 0.69-0.75). Unsupervised analysis identified four tumor cell morphotypes, revealing intra- and inter-patient morphological heterogeneity and longitudinal variation in morphotype composition. Genomic profiling of enriched tumor cell fractions by low-pass whole-genome sequencing (n = 26 samples) and whole-exome sequencing (n = 24 samples) identified copy-number alterations and somatic mutations, with tumor fraction influencing genomic signal strength. Comparisons of genomic profiles from tumor cell-enriched fractions with matched effusion cell-free DNA and solid tumors revealed shared genomic alterations, providing orthogonal support for tumor origin and relatedness, while differences across analytes revealed genomic divergence and tumor heterogeneity. ConclusionAI-powered analysis leverages single-cell morphology for tumor cell identification and label-free enrichment, while integration with genomic profiling enables simultaneous interrogation of phenotypic and genomic heterogeneity in malignant effusions. This approach expands the potential of malignant effusions for liquid biopsy applications and biomarker development and discovery.

infographic.key_insight: AI-guided single-cell imaging and label-free enrichment revealed morphological and genomic heterogeneity in metastatic breast cancer cells from malignant effusions.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This research approach could enable molecular characterization of accessible metastatic samples, but clinical utility and treatment-selection benefits remain unproven.
method: Applied a pre-trained deep learning model to single-cell brightfield images to estimate tumor cell fractions and characterize morphology.
Used morphology-guided microfluidics for label-free tumor cell enrichment.
Profiled copy-number alterations and mutations, comparing enriched cells with available matched effusion cell-free DNA and solid tumors.
infographic.evidence_signal: In 10 patients, imaging identified putative tumor cells across 25 samples (median tumor cell fraction, 5.4%) and four tumor morphotypes; genomic profiling showed shared alterations and divergence across analytes.
infographic.watch_item: The small cohort and tumor-fraction-dependent genomic signal warrant broader validation before clinical implementation.
infographic.paper_title: AI-powered single-cell imaging and morphology-guided label-free enrichment reveal tumor heterogeneity, genomic relatedness, and divergence in malignant effusions

title: Suvorexant Inversely Affects Phosphorylated Tau in Human Cerebrospinal Fluid and Plasma
authors: Pedersen, T. J.; Yu, J.; Li, A.; Ibanez, L.; Bubu, O. M.; Lucey, B. P.
abstract: Alzheimer disease (AD) is characterized by amyloid-{beta} plaques and neurofibrillary tangles of tau. Suvorexant, a dual orexin receptor antagonist, was previously shown to acutely reduce the ratio of phosphorylated tau-181 to unphosphorylated tau-181 (pT181/T181) in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). However, its effects on plasma pT181/T181 and broader proteomic networks remain unknown. Here, we conducted a secondary analysis of samples from a randomized, placebo-controlled trial of 25 participants receiving placebo or suvorexant 20 mg. Paired CSF and plasma samples were collected longitudinally via indwelling intrathecal and intravenous catheters. Plasma AD biomarkers were quantified by mass spectrometry, and proteomic profiling was performed using the SomaScan 11K assay on samples from hours 0, 16, and 24. Suvorexant increased pT181/T181 in plasma while decreasing it in CSF between 08:00-16:00. At the pathway level, suvorexant increased the extracellular abundance of proteins associated with translation, RNA binding, cytoskeletal organization and endosomal sorting, centrally at 16 hours and peripherally at 24 hours, and decreased cytokine and receptor-ligand signaling and serine protease activity in plasma at 24 hours. As plasma biomarkers are increasingly used for clinical screening and trial enrollment, factors that influence their levels, including medications, must be identified and their effects on interpretation understood.

infographic.key_insight: Suvorexant increased the phosphorylated-to-unphosphorylated tau-181 ratio in plasma while decreasing it in cerebrospinal fluid, revealing opposite biomarker responses across compartments.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Medication-related shifts in plasma tau biomarkers may complicate interpretation in Alzheimer disease screening and trial enrollment; this study did not examine AI or cancer drug discovery.
method: Secondary analysis of a randomized, placebo-controlled trial involving 25 participants receiving placebo or suvorexant 20 mg.
Longitudinal paired cerebrospinal fluid and plasma sampling, with plasma Alzheimer biomarkers measured by mass spectrometry.
SomaScan 11K proteomic profiling at hours 0, 16, and 24.
infographic.evidence_signal: Between 08:00 and 16:00, tau-181 phosphorylation ratios shifted in opposite directions in plasma and cerebrospinal fluid, alongside compartment- and time-dependent proteomic changes.
infographic.watch_item: This small, acute secondary analysis does not establish long-term biomarker effects or clinical benefit in Alzheimer disease.
infographic.paper_title: Suvorexant Inversely Affects Phosphorylated Tau in Human Cerebrospinal Fluid and Plasma

title: Phenome-wide and proteomic analysis of APOE alleles across different ancestries in the All of Us Research Program
authors: Mejia Garcia, A.; Valderrama-Carmona, P.; Zheng, T. M.; Wang, Z.; Tsao, H. M.; Jung, J.; Orozco, C. A.; Su, C.-Y.; Zhou, S.
abstract: BackgroundApolipoprotein E (APOE) {varepsilon}4 is the strongest common genetic risk factor for Alzheimers disease and a determinant of cardiometabolic risk, yet studies of APOE genotypes with disease associations and plasma proteomic signatures have been primarily restricted to European-ancestry cohorts. MethodsWe performed a phenome-wide association study of APOE genotype in 367,757 All of Us participants across six genetic ancestry groups. APOE alleles were tested against 2,632 phenotypes using an ordinal Alzheimers-disease-risk hierarchy ({varepsilon}2/{varepsilon}2 < {varepsilon}2/{varepsilon}3 < {varepsilon}3/{varepsilon}3 < {varepsilon}2/{varepsilon}4 < {varepsilon}3/{varepsilon}4 < {varepsilon}4/{varepsilon}4), adjusted for age, sex at birth, EHR length, and 16 genetic principal components. Sex- and ancestry-stratified analyses used Cochrans Q for heterogeneity. We evaluated {varepsilon}2 and {varepsilon}4 dosage effects on plasma protein levels in 9,132 participants across five ancestries. FindingsWe identified 27 phenotypes associated with APOE, mainly in neurological and lipid-related traits. Five lipid-related traits showed sex heterogeneity, with larger effects in females. Nine associations showed ancestry-specific effects. APOE {varepsilon}4 showed stronger protection against fatty liver disease in East Asians with lack of protection in African ancestry; and larger dementia risk for Europeans. Finally, SNAP25 was identified as positively associated with APOE {varepsilon}4 dosage across ancestries, and CDC42EP1, APOA1 and ITGB5 shown associations with APOE {varepsilon}2/{varepsilon}4 specifically in non-European populations. InterpretationAncestry-heterogeneous APOE effects, particularly for liver and dementia phenotypes, argue for ancestry-aware interpretation of APOE-based risk. Plasma SNAP25 is a candidate ancestry-portable biomarker of APOE-{varepsilon}4 effects, and ancestry-specific proteins nominate mechanisms for the observed phenotypic heterogeneity. Research in context Evidence before this studyThe APOE {varepsilon}4 variant is an established genetic risk factor for hyperlipidemia, Alzheimers disease, dementia, ischemic heart disease and, more recently, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease. Prior phenome-wide association studies (PheWAS) of APOE have been conducted largely in European-ancestry cohorts. A recent APOE PheWAS in the All of Us Research Program (n = 181,880) identified 17 Bonferroni-significant phenotypes and preliminary evidence of ancestry heterogeneity for hyperlipidemia and mild cognitive impairment, but statistical power in non-European groups limited systematic characterization of ancestry-specific effects. Recent plasma proteomic studies have described APOE-associated protein signatures shared with neurodegenerative diseases, but these were confined to European-ancestry participants, leaving open whether such signatures generalize across ancestries. Added value of this studyUsing the All of Us v9 release, we approximately doubled the sample size of the prior APOE PheWAS in this cohort (n = 367,757 across six ancestry groups, including [~]146,000 non-European participants), enabling the first well-powered assessment of ancestry heterogeneity of APOE effects. We identify 27 Bonferroni-significant phecodes, 11 novel compared to the previous APOE PheWAS in All of Us -- including vascular dementia, dementia with Lewy bodies, and angina pectoris. We detect significant sex heterogeneity for five lipid-related phecodes and significant ancestry heterogeneity for nine phecodes, including stronger protection against fatty liver and chronic liver disease in East Asian participants and larger dementia risk in European participants. Complementing the phenotypic analysis, we present the first ancestry-stratified plasma proteomic characterization of APOE genotypes (n = 9,132), identifying SNAP25 as a robust APOE-{varepsilon}4-associated protein across ancestries and ancestry-specific signals for IL32, CDC42EP1, APOA1, and ITGB5. Implications of all the available evidenceAPOE-associated risk estimates derived predominantly from European-ancestry data may not transfer directly to other populations, and our findings support incorporating ancestry into the interpretation and calibration of APOE-based risk prediction. The ancestry-heterogeneous protection against liver disease and the parallel APOA1 signal absent in East and South Asian participants together offer a mechanistic hypothesis linking APOE-driven lipid partitioning to hepatic outcomes. Plasma SNAP25 is proposed as an accessible, ancestry-portable biomarker of APOE-{varepsilon}4 effects and Alzheimers disease progression. Ancestry-specific proteins (IL32 and CDC42EP1 in African ancestry, ITGB5 in Admixed American ancestry) constitute potential drivers of ancestry heterogeneity in APOE-related disease risk.

infographic.key_insight: APOE associations with dementia, liver disease and plasma proteins varied by ancestry, while SNAP25 increased with ε4 dosage across ancestries.
infographic.clinical_relevance: These findings support ancestry-aware research into APOE-related risk and biomarkers, but do not establish clinical tests or treatment strategies.
method: Tested APOE genotype associations with 2,632 phenotypes across six genetic ancestry groups.
Adjusted for demographic and genetic covariates and assessed sex- and ancestry-related heterogeneity.
Evaluated APOE ε2 and ε4 dosage associations with plasma proteins across five ancestries.
infographic.evidence_signal: The study included 367,757 participants in phenome-wide analyses and 9,132 in proteomic analyses, identifying 27 associated phenotypes and nine associations with ancestry-specific effects.
infographic.watch_item: This observational APOE study is not AI cancer drug discovery research; its associations and candidate biomarkers require independent validation.
infographic.paper_title: Phenome-wide and proteomic analysis of APOE alleles across different ancestries in the All of Us Research Program

title: Investigating AI's potential in risk-stratifying lung cancer screenings for extending screening intervals and reducing workload: A retrospective analysis of a tertiary hospital cohort
authors: Nowroozi, A.; Bondarenko, M.; Brar, S. S.; Haas, B.; Brown, J.; Rustagi, A.; Graham, B.; Hudson, M.; Su, G.; Yala, A.; Sohn, J. H.
abstract: ObjectiveWe aimed to 1) evaluate whether AI algorithms could identify a very low-risk sub-population Lung-RADS 1/2 cases suitable for a safe switch to biennial screening, and 2) externally validate Sybil, an imaging-based deep learning lung cancer risk prediction tool. Materials and methodsWe gathered all lung cancer screenings (LCSs) from a tertiary safety-net hospital (n=3120, up to September 2024), manually extracted relevant clinical data, and analyzed Sybils performance across various subgroups, with a specific focus on Lung-RADS 1 and 2 cases. We simulated LCS interval extension using Sybil and the Brock model risk scores calibrated on a subset of the National Lung Screening Trial (NLST). Confidence intervals were obtained through bootstrapping. ResultsThe median follow-up was 2.3 years (interquartile range 1.5-3.1), with a total 6-year cancer incidence rate of 2.3% (72/3120). Lung-RADS 1 and 2 cases comprised 90.5% of our scans. Sybils overall area under the curve (AUC) ranged from 0.819 to 0.912; while its 2-year AUC for Lung-RADS 1 and 2 cases was 0.746. In the screening interval extension simulation, calibrating for a 30% shift to biennial screening translated into 33.8% of negative screens in our data being safely extended using Sybil, with no delayed cancers. The Brock model demonstrated an AUC of 0.513 on our data, with a sensitivity of 18.2% using the 1.5% threshold. ConclusionSybil has the potential to safely extend LCS intervals for low-risk individuals, reducing radiology workload and opening spots for life-saving new screenings. Key pointsO_LIWe investigated whether AI risk stratification tools could identify the lowest-risk individuals undergoing lung cancer screening suitable for switching to a biennial screening schedule. C_LIO_LIIn our simulations, Sybil reduced follow-up screening load by at least 30% through switching the lowest-risk Lung-RADS 1 and 2 cases to biennial screening without delayed cancer diagnoses. C_LIO_LIVery low-risk individuals, as predicted by AI algorithms, could potentially be placed on biennial screening schedules, reducing radiology department workload and freeing time for new patients. C_LI

infographic.key_insight: In a retrospective simulation, Sybil identified 33.8% of negative lung cancer screens for biennial rather than annual screening, with no delayed cancer diagnoses observed.
infographic.clinical_relevance: AI-guided screening intervals could reduce follow-up imaging workload and expand screening capacity, but prospective validation is needed before clinical adoption.
method: Analyzed 3,120 lung cancer screens from a tertiary safety-net hospital.
Externally evaluated Sybil, focusing on low-risk Lung-RADS 1/2 screens.
Simulated interval extension using Sybil and Brock risk scores calibrated on an NLST subset.
infographic.evidence_signal: Sybil's 2-year AUC was 0.746 for Lung-RADS 1/2 screens; the cohort had 72 cancers and a median follow-up of 2.3 years.
infographic.watch_item: The single-center, retrospective simulation does not establish the safety of biennial screening in prospective practice.
infographic.paper_title: Investigating AI's potential in risk-stratifying lung cancer screenings for extending screening intervals and reducing workload: A retrospective analysis of a tertiary hospital cohort

title: Epilepsy Lateralization by Elastic Net Regularization of a Diffusion Tensor Imaging Biomarker using Machine Learning
authors: Lepping, R. J.; Pearl, M.; Chen, X.; Hu, J.; Li, Y.; Akhter, M.; Farrenburg, M.; Landazuri, P.; Pearson, C. M.
abstract: ObjectiveAccurate lateralization of the epileptogenic focus is essential for presurgical evaluation of patients with drug-resistant epilepsy. This study examined whether diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) measures of white matter microstructure, combined with clinical and demographic variables, could classify epilepsy lateralization using machine learning. MethodsWe present a retrospective analysis of 334 adult patients undergoing presurgical epilepsy evaluation at the University of Kansas Health System. Fractional anisotropy (FA) and mean diffusivity (MD) were extracted from 36 bilateral white matter tracts and combined with clinical and demographic variables. Several supervised machine learning approaches were evaluated, with elastic net logistic regression selected for detailed analysis. Models classified right-sided, left-sided, and bilateral or generalized epilepsy. Performance was evaluated with area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity as performance metrics. ResultsElastic net models demonstrated good discrimination across classification tasks, with AUC values ranging from 0.76 to 0.88. The strongest performance distinguished left-sided epilepsy from bilateral or generalized epilepsy (AUC = 0.88; accuracy = 0.90; sensitivity = 0.90; specificity = 0.89). Discrimination between unilateral epilepsy and bilateral or generalized epilepsy was also good (AUC = 0.83). Classification of right-sided versus left-sided epilepsy demonstrated lower performance (AUC = 0.76). SignificanceDTI-derived white matter features analyzed using a machine learning approach may provide complementary information for epilepsy lateralization during presurgical evaluation. Further studies incorporating other pre-surgical evaluation data into the machine learning model are needed to establish the clinical utility of this approach. Key PointsO_LIA machine learning model was tested using diffusion tensor imaging and clinical data to retrospectively classify epilepsy lateralization. C_LIO_LIOur model balanced sensitivity and specificity in epilepsy localization, suggesting potential as an interpretable surgical decision tool. C_LIO_LIFindings support the hypothesis that white matter tracts contain useful information about seizure propagation to distal brain regions. C_LIO_LIFurther model validation is needed before this can be used as a clinical tool. C_LI

infographic.key_insight: Elastic net machine learning combined diffusion MRI and clinical data to classify epilepsy lateralization, with AUCs of 0.76–0.88; this study concerns epilepsy, not cancer drug discovery.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The approach may complement presurgical epilepsy evaluation, but its clinical utility remains unestablished.
method: Retrospective analysis of 334 adults undergoing presurgical epilepsy evaluation.
Combined fractional anisotropy and mean diffusivity from 36 bilateral white matter tracts with clinical and demographic variables.
Evaluated supervised classifiers, focusing on elastic net logistic regression for lateralization.
infographic.evidence_signal: Left-sided versus bilateral or generalized epilepsy showed the strongest discrimination (AUC 0.88; accuracy 0.90), while right-sided versus left-sided classification achieved AUC 0.76.
infographic.watch_item: Single-center retrospective findings require further validation and integration with other presurgical data before clinical use.
infographic.paper_title: Epilepsy Lateralization by Elastic Net Regularization of a Diffusion Tensor Imaging Biomarker using Machine Learning

title: Alzheimer's disease-related cerebrospinal fluid Biomarkers in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis: Real-World Associations with Disease Status, Cognition and Tofersen Response
authors: Eberle, F.; Bersen, S.; Rachel, F.; Widmann, C.; Weydt, P.; Castro-Gomez, S.
abstract: Background and ObjectivesAmyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a neurodegenerative disease primarily affecting motor neurons but also frequently involving cognitive impairment. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) measurements of {beta}-amyloid peptides (A{beta}40, A{beta}42), tau proteins, and neurofilaments are clinically established biomarkers in Alzheimers disease (AD). Emerging evidence suggests that AD-related pathological changes and AD-related biomarkers may appear in ALS, yet their diagnostic and prognostic significance remains incompletely understood. MethodsIn this retrospective study, we analyzed clinical and CSF biomarker data from patients with ALS, AD, Huntingtons disease (HD), and other disease controls from real-world clinical settings. The dataset comprised A{beta}40, A{beta}42, total tau (t-Tau), phosphorylated tau181 (pTau181), phosphorylated neurofilament heavy chain (pNfH), and relevant serum markers as well as clinical and cognitive status measurements. Additionally, longitudinal CSF sampling over one year was evaluated in three ALS patients receiving tofersen treatment. ResultsIn this real-world cohort, AD-related CSF biomarkers demonstrated no diagnostic value for distinguishing ALS from other neurodegenerative conditions. However, A{beta}40, A{beta}42, and pTau181 levels correlated positively with ALS Functional Rating Scale (ALSFRS-R) global score and serum Creatine Kinase MB (CK-MB) concentrations. At the same time, a higher A{beta}42/A{beta}40 ratio was associated with better memory performance on the Edinburgh Cognitive and Behavioural ALS Screen (ECAS). In tofersen-treated cases, AD-related biomarkers gradually declined during follow-up. DiscussionThese findings suggest that elevated CSF AD-associated biomarkers in ALS may reflect preserved functional and cognitive status and exhibited parallel declines during follow-up in three tofersen-treated patients, supporting their further prospective evaluation as exploratory markers of therapeutic responsiveness. infographic.key_insight: In ALS, higher levels of selected Alzheimer’s-related CSF biomarkers were associated with better functional or memory performance, but did not distinguish ALS from other neurodegenerative conditions.
infographic.clinical_relevance: These biomarkers warrant prospective study as exploratory indicators of ALS status and treatment response, not as established diagnostic or treatment-guiding tools.
method: Retrospective analysis of real-world clinical and CSF data from ALS, Alzheimer’s disease, Huntington’s disease, and other disease controls.
Assessed amyloid peptides, tau proteins, neurofilaments, serum markers, and functional and cognitive measures.
Evaluated longitudinal CSF samples over one year in three tofersen-treated ALS patients.
infographic.evidence_signal: Aβ40, Aβ42, and pTau181 correlated positively with ALSFRS-R and serum CK-MB; a higher Aβ42/Aβ40 ratio correlated with better memory, while Alzheimer’s-related biomarkers declined during tofersen follow-up.
infographic.watch_item: The retrospective associations and three-patient treatment series cannot establish causality or validate biomarkers of therapeutic response; this study concerns ALS, not AI-driven cancer drug discovery.
infographic.paper_title: Alzheimer's disease-related cerebrospinal fluid Biomarkers in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis: Real-World Associations with Disease Status, Cognition and Tofersen Response

title: Physiological Waveform Features Based Aging Clocks Associate with Cardiovascular Disease
authors: Pal, R.; Barney, A.; Cannesson, M.
abstract: Aging affects the morphology of photoplethysmography (PPG) and arterial blood pressure (ABP) waveforms. Here, we demonstrate that machine learning (ML) models trained on features derived from PPG or ABP waveforms can predict an individual's age. We further investigated whether the discrepancy between predicted and chronological age (Age-Gap) could serve as a measure of cardiovascular health by testing its association with cardiovascular disease (CVD). From a large perioperative dataset of 17,327 surgical patients, high-fidelity PPG and ABP waveforms were analyzed, and over 840 time-, frequency-, and statistical-domain features per cardiac cycle were extracted using a signal-processing-based tool. These features were then used to develop ML-based aging clocks, PPGAge and ABPAge, trained on PPG and ABP features, respectively. For each aging clock, we evaluated five ML models: Light Gradient Boosting Machine (LightGBM), eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Random Forest, Lasso, and Elastic Net. Individuals were classified as having accelerated, normal, or delayed aging based on their Age-Gap relative to the model-specific mean absolute error (MAE, rounded up to the nearest whole year): accelerated aging was defined as Age-Gap [≥] +MAE, normal aging as -MAE [≤] Age-Gap < +MAE, and delayed aging as Age-Gap < -MAE. LightGBM provided the best age predictions for both aging clocks, with Pearson correlation coefficients (r) of 0.92 and 0.92 and R-squared values of 0.81 and 0.82 for PPGAge and ABPAge, respectively. Moreover, we found that accelerated aging was significantly associated with higher odds of CVD for both aging clocks, PPGAge (odds ratio, 1.87 [95% CI, 1.59-2.21], p<0.001) and ABPAge (odds ratio, 2.28 [95% CI, 1.51-3.43], p<0.001). Additionally, delayed aging was significantly associated with lower odds of CVD for PPGAge (odds ratio, 0.68 [95% CI, 0.58-0.80], p<0.001). Our findings suggest that aging clocks based on high-fidelity PPG or ABP waveform features may serve as novel biomarkers for identifying individuals with higher odds of CVD.

infographic.key_insight: Machine-learning clocks derived from physiological waveforms predicted age, with accelerated waveform aging associated with higher odds of cardiovascular disease—not cancer drug discovery.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Waveform-based aging clocks may offer investigational cardiovascular health biomarkers, but these findings do not establish clinical utility.
method: Extracted over 840 time-, frequency-, and statistical-domain features per cardiac cycle from PPG and arterial blood pressure waveforms.
Compared five machine-learning models to build PPGAge and ABPAge aging clocks.
Classified aging using predicted-minus-chronological age relative to model-specific error thresholds and tested associations with cardiovascular disease.
infographic.evidence_signal: Among 17,327 surgical patients, LightGBM achieved age-prediction correlations of 0.92 for both clocks; accelerated aging was associated with higher cardiovascular disease odds for PPGAge (OR 1.87, 95% CI 1.59–2.21) and ABPAge (OR 2.28, 95% CI 1.51–3.43).
infographic.watch_item: Findings from a perioperative cohort require external validation before generalization to other populations or routine clinical use.
infographic.paper_title: Physiological Waveform Features Based Aging Clocks Associate with Cardiovascular Disease

title: Alzheimers disease and psychiatric polygenic risk are disease-specific and independent of plasma biomarkers in a real-world young-onset dementia cohort.
authors: Bhalala, O. G.; Wang, L.; Gerring, Z. F.; Han, J.; Kang, M. J.; Trounson, B. O.; Loi, S. M.; Velakoulis, D.; Eratne, D.; Bahlo, M.; The MiND Study Group,
abstract: BackgroundYoung-onset dementia is frequently misdiagnosed, particularly where neurodegenerative and primary psychiatric disorders (PPD) overlap. Plasma biomarkers measure current pathology, whereas polygenic risk scores (PRS) capture lifelong genetic risk. Whether PRS derived from late-onset and population samples transfer to young-onset presentations, and how they relate to plasma biomarkers, is unknown. MethodsWe studied 687 participants of European ancestry from the Markers in Neuropsychiatric Disorders (MiND) Study, a prospective young-onset neuropsychiatry cohort: 195 healthy controls (HC), 283 PPD, 55 Alzheimers disease (AD) and 154 non-AD neurodegenerative disease (oNDG). PRS for AD, a cross-disorder psychiatric factor (PSY), frontotemporal dementia, Lewy body dementia and Parkinsons disease were computed with PRS-CS, excluding the APOE locus. Plasma NfL, GFAP and p-tau217 were available for 332 participants. Models were adjusted for age, sex and APOE {varepsilon}4 dose. ResultsRelative to HC, the AD PRS was associated with AD (OR 1.69 per SD, 95% CI 1.17-2.45) but not PPD (0.95, 0.77-1.16). The PSY PRS showed the reciprocal pattern (PPD 1.29, 1.05-1.58; AD 1.00, 0.72-1.40). No PRS was associated with any plasma protein. In distinguishing PPD from oNDG, NfL was the strongest discriminator (OR 2.15, 1.62-2.83). The AD PRS was also associated with oNDG (1.38, 1.11-1.71), without improving discrimination (AUC 0.764 for NfL alone versus 0.773 combined). ConclusionIn young-onset presentations, AD and psychiatric polygenic risk are disease-specific and independent of plasma biomarkers of neurodegeneration. Their combined diagnostic value requires evaluation in larger, longitudinal pre-clinical cohorts.

infographic.key_insight: In a young-onset neuropsychiatry cohort, Alzheimer’s and psychiatric polygenic risk showed distinct disease associations, with neither associated with measured plasma biomarkers.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Genetic risk and plasma biomarkers may provide different information, but their combined diagnostic value remains unproven.
method: Analyzed 687 European-ancestry participants: 195 controls, 283 with primary psychiatric disorders, 55 with Alzheimer’s disease and 154 with other neurodegenerative diseases.
Computed five polygenic risk scores excluding APOE; adjusted models for age, sex and APOE ε4 dose.
Assessed plasma NfL, GFAP and p-tau217 in 332 participants.
infographic.evidence_signal: Alzheimer’s PRS was associated with Alzheimer’s disease (OR 1.69 per SD), psychiatric PRS with psychiatric disorders (OR 1.29), and adding Alzheimer’s PRS to NfL did not improve discrimination of psychiatric versus other neurodegenerative disease (AUC 0.764 versus 0.773).
infographic.watch_item: European-ancestry sampling and small diagnostic subgroups limit generalizability; larger longitudinal cohorts are needed before clinical implementation.
infographic.paper_title: Alzheimers disease and psychiatric polygenic risk are disease-specific and independent of plasma biomarkers in a real-world young-onset dementia cohort.

title: CSF PrP-amyloid seeding predicts clinical onset in inherited prion disease
authors: Mok, T. H.; Nihat, A.; Vallabh, S. M.; Noa, B.; Omer, N.; Geschwind, M.; Arnold, S. E.; Minikel, E. V.; Collinge, J.; Mead, S.
abstract: Silent proteopathic seed propagation is hypothesised to precede neurodegenerative disease, but direct evidence that it signals near-term clinical conversion in humans is lacking. In prion disease, a prototypic disorder of proteopathic seeding, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) real-time quaking-induced conversion (RT-QuIC) offers a direct measure of prion protein amyloid seeding activity. We analysed longitudinal CSF RT-QuIC data from 94 PRNP E200K mutation carriers across international natural history cohorts to determine whether seeding status predicts clinical conversion. Eleven carriers developed inherited prion disease; all showed at least one positive RT-QuIC result before onset. First positivity appeared a median of 2.0 years prior to symptoms (IQR 1.3-3.3; range 0.2-4.8). Landmark analyses showed RT-QuIC positivity identified a markedly increased short-term conversion risk, whereas persistently asymptomatic carriers remained negative throughout follow-up. These findings establish CSF RT-QuIC positivity as a biomarker-defined state of incipient conversion in E200K carriers, informing risk stratification and preventive trial design.

infographic.key_insight: CSF prion protein amyloid seeding detected by RT-QuIC preceded symptoms and signaled near-term disease onset in PRNP E200K carriers.
infographic.clinical_relevance: This prion disease study—not AI cancer drug discovery—could inform risk stratification and preventive trial design in E200K carriers.
method: Analyzed longitudinal CSF RT-QuIC results from 94 PRNP E200K carriers across international natural history cohorts.
Used landmark analyses to assess whether seeding positivity predicted clinical conversion.
infographic.evidence_signal: All 11 carriers who developed disease had a positive RT-QuIC result before onset, with first positivity a median of 2.0 years before symptoms; persistently asymptomatic carriers remained negative during follow-up.
infographic.watch_item: Only 11 clinical conversions were observed, and applicability beyond E200K carriers requires validation.
infographic.paper_title: CSF PrP-amyloid seeding predicts clinical onset in inherited prion disease
